```{r}
#| label: cleanup
#| include: false
# make sure we're starting clean
unlink("ingest-predictors.evolanddb", recursive = TRUE)
set.seed(143)
```

*Note: this how-to guide assumes that you know the basic `evoland.plus` workflow from the [tutorial](evoland.plus.html), and that you have worked with `terra` rasters and vectors before.*

Predictors usually come as files: GeoTIFFs of terrain or noise exposure, vector layers of protected areas or roads.
None of them are on the grid of your model.
This guide shows how to bring such files onto the coordinate points of an `evoland_db`, and how to keep track of where they came from.

Real predictor data is large: the Swiss noise maps used in an earlier version of this guide cover all of Switzerland at 10 m.
So that this guide runs anywhere, we write small synthetic files to a temporary directory first and then ingest them the way you would ingest downloaded files.
@sec-real-data shows the same steps on real, remote data.

We'll use the following packages:

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| output: false
library(evoland.plus)
library(data.table)
library(terra)
```

# Setting up the domain

We need a database with coordinate points, periods and some observed land use.
As in the tutorial, `synthetic_landscape()` simulates a landscape of 40 x 40 cells of 100 m at the origin of Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), and its grid becomes our spatial domain.

```{r}
#| label: create-db
landscape <- synthetic_landscape(n_periods = 3, n_cells = 40)

db <- evoland_db$new(path = "ingest-predictors.evolanddb")

db$coords_t <- create_coords_t_square(
  epsg = 3857L,
  extent = terra::ext(landscape$lulc),
  resolution = 100
)

db$periods_t <- create_periods_t(
  period_length_str = "P10Y",
  start_observed = "2000-01-01",
  end_observed = "2030-01-01",
  end_extrapolated = "2040-01-01"
)

db$lulc_meta_t <- create_lulc_meta_t(list(
  forest = list(pretty_name = "Forest", src_classes = 1),
  arable = list(pretty_name = "Arable land", src_classes = 2),
  urban = list(pretty_name = "Urban areas", src_classes = 3),
  lake = list(pretty_name = "Lake", src_classes = 4)
))

db$lulc_data_t <-
  extract_using_coords_t(landscape$lulc, db$coords_t)[,
    .(id_coord, id_period = as.integer(sub("id_period=", "", layer)), src_class = value)
  ][db$lulc_meta_long_v, on = "src_class", nomatch = NULL][,
    .(id_run = 0L, id_period, id_lulc, id_coord)
  ] |>
  as_lulc_data_t()

db$extent
```

The domain holds 1600 coordinate points.
`db$extent` spans the points themselves, i.e. the cell centers from 50 m to 3950 m, not the cell edges.

Rasters must be brought onto this grid before we read values at the points, so we build an empty raster template whose cells are centered on the coordinate points.
Because `db$extent` spans the cell centers, we widen it by half a cell on each side to get the cell edges.

```{r}
#| label: grid-template
resolution <- attr(db$coords_t, "resolution")
template <- terra::rast(
  terra::extend(db$extent, resolution / 2), # from cell centers to cell edges
  resolution = resolution,
  crs = "EPSG:3857"
)
template
```

# Writing synthetic source files

We now write three files, each deliberately off the model grid in a different way:

- `elevation.tif`, a continuous raster in geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326) at about 22 m;
- `soils.tif`, a categorical raster in EPSG:3857 at 50 m, whose cell edges are shifted by 30 m against the model grid;
- `infrastructure.gpkg`, a GeoPackage with a polygon layer of protected areas and a line layer of roads.

`soils.tif` holds integer codes with a label for each code.
GDAL stores such labels in a sidecar file next to the GeoTIFF, `soils.tif.aux.xml`, so the soil data consists of two files.

```{r}
#| label: write-rasters
source_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "predictor-sources")
dir.create(source_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# a hill in the north east and some ripples, on a grid in degrees
elevation <- terra::rast(
  terra::ext(-0.005, 0.041, -0.005, 0.041),
  resolution = 0.0002,
  crs = "EPSG:4326"
)
xy <- terra::crds(elevation)
values(elevation) <-
  420 +
  300 * exp(-((xy[, 1] - 0.028)^2 + (xy[, 2] - 0.03)^2) / 2e-4) +
  15 * sin(xy[, 1] * 900) +
  rnorm(nrow(xy), sd = 2)
names(elevation) <- "elevation"
terra::writeRaster(elevation, file.path(source_dir, "elevation.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)

# soil codes 1 to 4 in smooth patches, cut at the quartiles of a smoothed random field
soils <- terra::rast(terra::ext(-130, 4170, -130, 4170), resolution = 50, crs = "EPSG:3857")
values(soils) <- rnorm(terra::ncell(soils))
soils <- terra::focal(soils, w = 15, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
soils <-
  terra::classify(soils, stats::quantile(values(soils), 0:4 / 4), include.lowest = TRUE) |>
  (\(x) x + 1)() |>
  stats::setNames("soil")
levels(soils) <- data.frame(id = 1:4, soil = c("gravel", "loam", "clay", "peat"))
terra::writeRaster(
  soils,
  file.path(source_dir, "soils.tif"),
  datatype = "INT1U",
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

The vector layers are built from coordinates, as if digitized:
a nature reserve and a larger landscape protection area that do not overlap, and a motorway and a main road.

```{r}
#| label: write-vectors
protected_areas <- terra::vect(
  c(
    "POLYGON ((2600 2500, 3700 2600, 3800 3700, 2900 3900, 2500 3300, 2600 2500))",
    "POLYGON ((300 2400, 1800 2100, 2200 3200, 1500 3900, 200 3600, 300 2400))"
  ),
  crs = "EPSG:3857"
)
protected_areas$category <- c("nature reserve", "landscape protection")

roads <- terra::vect(
  list(
    cbind(c(-100, 1200, 2600, 4100), c(700, 1000, 1500, 1300)),
    cbind(c(1300, 1400, 1100, 1200), c(-100, 1500, 2800, 4100))
  ),
  type = "lines",
  crs = "EPSG:3857"
)
roads$class <- c("motorway", "main road")

infrastructure_path <- file.path(source_dir, "infrastructure.gpkg")
unlink(infrastructure_path)
terra::writeVector(protected_areas, infrastructure_path, layer = "protected_areas")
terra::writeVector(roads, infrastructure_path, layer = "roads", insert = TRUE)

list.files(source_dir)
```

From here on, the files are all we use.

# Recording and fetching sources

Each predictor in `pred_meta_t` can list its `sources`: a URL and the MD5 checksum of each file it was derived from.
`download_and_verify()` takes such a table, downloads every file into a cache directory with one folder per checksum, and warns if a file no longer matches its checksum.
Files that are already in the cache are not downloaded again.

`download_and_verify()` fetches exactly the URLs it is given.
A sidecar file such as `soils.tif.aux.xml` is not fetched along with its GeoTIFF, so we list it as a source of its own; a predictor can have any number of sources.

Our files are local, so their URLs use the `file://` scheme, which `download_and_verify()` handles like any other.
In a real project, the URLs point to a persistent archive, ideally one with a DOI, and are written out by hand together with the checksums the provider publishes, as the comments show.

```{r}
#| label: fetch-sources
source_files <- file.path(
  source_dir,
  c("elevation.tif", "soils.tif", "soils.tif.aux.xml", "infrastructure.gpkg")
)
sources <- data.table(
  url = paste0("file://", source_files),
  # url = c(
  #   "https://example.org/archive/elevation.tif",
  #   "ftp://ftp.example.org/soils/soils.tif",
  #   "ftp://ftp.example.org/soils/soils.tif.aux.xml",
  #   "https://example.org/archive/infrastructure.gpkg"
  # ),
  md5sum = unname(tools::md5sum(source_files))
)

fetched <- download_and_verify(sources, target_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "evoland-cache"))
fetched[, .(local_filename, checksum_matches = md5sum == md5sum_actual)]
```

All four checksums match, and `local_path` in `fetched` points to the cached copies we read below.

```{r}
#| label: local-paths
#| include: false
local_path <- function(filename) fetched[local_filename == filename, local_path]
```

# Raster predictors

## Continuous: elevation

The elevation raster has a different coordinate reference system and a finer resolution than the model grid.
`terra::project()` onto the template does both steps at once; `method = "average"` takes the mean of all source cells that fall into a 100 m cell, rather than the value of whichever source cell happens to lie under the cell center.
`extract_using_coords_t()` then reads one value per coordinate point.

```{r}
#| label: ingest-elevation
elevation_at_coords <-
  terra::rast(local_path("elevation.tif")) |>
  terra::project(template, method = "average") |>
  extract_using_coords_t(db$coords_t)

db$add_predictor(
  pred_data_raw = elevation_at_coords[, .(id_coord, id_period = 0L, value)],
  name = "elevation",
  fill_value = NA,
  pretty_name = "Elevation",
  description = "Mean elevation within each cell",
  orig_format = "GeoTIFF, EPSG:4326, 0.0002 degrees",
  sources = sources[grepl("elevation", url)],
  unit = "m"
)

elevation_at_coords
```

Every coordinate point received a value.
Elevation does not change over time, so we store it under the static period `0`.
`add_predictor()` infers the `data_type` from the `value` column, here `float`.
There is no meaningful value to fill in for a missing elevation, so `fill_value` is `NA`.

## Categorical: soils

For the soil codes, averaging makes no sense.
`terra::resample()` with `method = "mode"` takes the most frequent code among the source cells that overlap a model cell, which handles both the coarser grid and the shifted cell edges.

GDAL only finds the labels if the sidecar sits next to the GeoTIFF.
The cache keeps every file in a folder named after its checksum, so the two cached files are in different folders.
We copy them into one working directory rather than into either cache folder, because `download_and_verify()` refuses a checksum folder that holds more than one file.

`extract_using_coords_t()` returns the labels of a categorical raster as text.
We turn them into a factor whose levels follow the codes in the file; `add_predictor()` stores the factor's integer codes and its levels in `pred_meta_t`, so that the codes can be turned back into a factor later.

```{r}
#| label: ingest-soils
soils_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "soils")
dir.create(soils_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
file.copy(c(local_path("soils.tif"), local_path("soils.tif.aux.xml")), soils_dir, overwrite = TRUE) |>
  invisible()
soils_rast <- terra::rast(file.path(soils_dir, "soils.tif"))
terra::levels(soils_rast)[[1]]

soils_at_coords <-
  terra::resample(soils_rast, template, method = "mode") |>
  extract_using_coords_t(db$coords_t)

# the codes run from 1 to 4, so the factor codes equal the codes in the file
soils_at_coords[, value := factor(value, levels = terra::levels(soils_rast)[[1]]$soil)]

db$add_predictor(
  pred_data_raw = soils_at_coords[, .(id_coord, id_period = 0L, value)],
  name = "soil",
  fill_value = NA,
  pretty_name = "Soil type",
  description = "Most frequent soil type within each cell",
  orig_format = "GeoTIFF with labels in an .aux.xml sidecar, EPSG:3857, 50 m",
  sources = sources[grepl("soils", url)]
)

soils_at_coords[, .N, by = value]
```

The labels survived the cache, and all four soil types occur in the domain, in roughly equal shares, as the quartile breaks above intend.
The `soil` predictor lists both files as its sources.

# Vector predictors

`evoland.plus` has no dedicated ingestion function for vector data; `terra` already covers what is needed at the coordinate points.
`extract_using_coords_t()` accepts a `SpatVector` as well as a `SpatRaster`, and for anything else we turn the coordinate points into a `SpatVector` ourselves.

## Polygons: protected areas

For polygons, `extract_using_coords_t()` returns the polygon attributes at each coordinate point that falls inside a polygon.
Points outside all polygons have no value and are dropped.

```{r}
#| label: ingest-protected-areas
protected_at_coords <-
  terra::vect(local_path("infrastructure.gpkg"), layer = "protected_areas") |>
  extract_using_coords_t(db$coords_t)

protected_at_coords[, .N, by = .(attribute, value)]
```

Only about a quarter of the coordinate points lie in a protected area.
The others are not missing data: they are unprotected.
Rather than writing a row for each of them, we declare this with `fill_value`, which applies to every coordinate point without a row.
For a factor predictor, the `fill_value` is a level, so we make sure `"unprotected"` is one.

```{r}
#| label: add-protected-areas
protected_at_coords[,
  value := factor(value, levels = c("unprotected", "landscape protection", "nature reserve"))
]

db$add_predictor(
  pred_data_raw = protected_at_coords[, .(id_coord, id_period = 0L, value)],
  name = "protection",
  fill_value = "unprotected",
  pretty_name = "Protection status",
  description = "Protected area category; unprotected outside protected areas",
  orig_format = "GeoPackage, polygons",
  sources = sources[grepl("infrastructure", url)]
)
```

## Lines: distance to the nearest road

A distance predictor needs a value at every point.
We turn the coordinate points into a `SpatVector` and compute the exact distance from each point to each road with `terra::distance()`, then keep the smallest per point.

```{r}
#| label: ingest-road-distance
coords <- db$coords_minimal
points <- terra::vect(as.matrix(coords[, .(lon, lat)]), crs = "EPSG:3857")
roads <- terra::vect(local_path("infrastructure.gpkg"), layer = "roads")

road_distance <- coords[, .(
  id_coord,
  id_period = 0L,
  value = terra::distance(points, roads) |> apply(1, min)
)]

db$add_predictor(
  pred_data_raw = road_distance,
  name = "distance_to_road",
  fill_value = NA,
  pretty_name = "Distance to the nearest road",
  description = "Euclidean distance from the coordinate point to the nearest motorway or main road",
  orig_format = "GeoPackage, lines",
  sources = sources[grepl("infrastructure", url)],
  unit = "m"
)

summary(road_distance$value)
```

The distances range from zero on a road to more than two kilometers in the north-east corner.
`terra::distance()` returns a matrix with one row per point and one column per road, so this approach suits domains of a few hundred thousand points and a modest number of features.
For larger problems, rasterize the lines onto the template with `terra::rasterize()` and compute the distance on the raster with `terra::distance()`; the result is exact to within one cell size and can be read with `extract_using_coords_t()` like any other raster.

# Checking the results

The predictor metadata now lists our four predictors with their data types, units and fill values, and the levels of the two factors.

```{r}
#| label: pred-meta
db$pred_meta_t[order(id_pred), .(id_pred, name, data_type, fill_value, unit)]
db$pred_meta_t[data_type == "factor", .(name, factor_levels)]
```

The `id_pred` follow the order in which we added the predictors.

`db$pred_sources_v` collects the distinct sources over all predictors.
This is the table to hand to `download_and_verify()` to rebuild a cache on a new machine.

```{r}
#| label: pred-sources
db$pred_sources_v
```

All predictor values are stored as doubles in a single `pred_data_t` table.
Converting them back to rasters with `tabular_to_raster()`, with the roads and protected areas drawn on top, is a quick visual check that each predictor landed where it should.

```{r}
#| label: plot-predictors
#| fig-asp: 0.9
db$pred_data_t[, .(id_coord, id_pred, value)] |>
  tabular_to_raster(db$coords_t, value_col = "value") |>
  stats::setNames(db$pred_meta_t[order(id_pred), pretty_name]) |>
  terra::plot(nc = 2, fun = \() {
    terra::polys(protected_areas, border = "grey40")
    terra::lines(roads, col = "red")
  })
```

The categorical maps show the stored integer codes, in the order of the factor levels.
The protection status map shows only the cells inside protected areas: the unprotected cells have no rows, and are filled in when the data is read for modeling.
`pred_wide_train_v()` does that read for one transition, here forest to arable land.
It casts each predictor back to its type and replaces missing values with the `fill_value`.

```{r}
#| label: wide-view
db$trans_meta_t <- create_trans_meta_t(db$trans_v(), min_cardinality_abs = 5)
id_forest_arable <- db$trans_meta_t[id_lulc_anterior == 1L & id_lulc_posterior == 2L, id_trans]

training <- db$pred_wide_train_v(id_trans = id_forest_arable)
str(training)
table(training$id_pred_3, useNA = "ifany")
```

The soil and protection columns (`id_pred_2`, `id_pred_3`) are factors again, and every row in `id_pred_3` has a protection status: the points without a row in `pred_data_t` came back as `unprotected`.

# Real data {#sec-real-data}

With real data, only the first steps differ: the sources are remote, and you take the URLs and checksums from the data provider.
The following chunk ingests the maximum of the Swiss daytime and nighttime road noise exposure maps (sonBASE) for a 1 km² domain near Zürich.
It is not run when this guide is built, because the two nationwide GeoTIFFs are too large to download every time the package documentation is built.

```{r}
#| label: real-noise-data
#| eval: false
noise_sources <- data.table(
  url = c(
    "https://data.geo.admin.ch/ch.bafu.laerm-strassenlaerm_tag/laerm-strassenlaerm_tag/laerm-strassenlaerm_tag_2056.tif",
    "https://data.geo.admin.ch/ch.bafu.laerm-strassenlaerm_nacht/laerm-strassenlaerm_nacht/laerm-strassenlaerm_nacht_2056.tif"
  ),
  md5sum = c("09791808dbf12fcde82182e70f2ebdfb", "6e79dc1d353751084e21dc6b61778b99")
)

db_ch <- evoland_db$new(path = "noisemodel.evolanddb")
db_ch$coords_t <- create_coords_t_square(
  epsg = 2056L,
  extent = terra::ext(2697000, 2698000, 1252000, 1253000),
  resolution = 100
)
template_ch <- terra::rast(
  terra::extend(db_ch$extent, 50), # from cell centers to cell edges
  resolution = 100,
  crs = "EPSG:2056"
)

# the cache directory defaults to getOption("evoland.plus.cachedir")
noise_files <- download_and_verify(noise_sources)

noise_at_coords <-
  lapply(noise_files$local_path, \(path) terra::rast(path) |> terra::crop(template_ch)) |>
  terra::rast() |>
  max(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  terra::resample(template_ch, method = "average") |>
  extract_using_coords_t(db_ch$coords_t)

db_ch$add_predictor(
  pred_data_raw = noise_at_coords[, .(id_coord, id_period = 0L, value)],
  name = "noise",
  fill_value = NA,
  pretty_name = "Maximum road noise exposure",
  description = "Maximum of the daytime and nighttime sonBASE road noise exposure",
  orig_format = "GeoTIFF, EPSG:2056, 10 m",
  sources = noise_sources,
  unit = "dB(A)"
)
```

Because the URLs and checksums are stored with the predictor, anyone with the database can fetch the same files again with `download_and_verify(db_ch$pred_sources_v)`, and is warned if the provider has changed them in the meantime.
